neighbours.summary: Fengheld's newest chapter house, an idyllic riverside site on a bend of the river Spree in the March of Lusatia, only ten miles from the agreed border with the Novgorod Tribunal; its founding caused the most recent boundary dispute between the two Tribunals. One maga lives here, mostly as a bear. Its aura is not given.

neighbours.name: Vysehrad Rock
neighbours.summary: A hilltop just south of Prague where, in the eighth century, the Gifted princess Libuse, granddaughter of Czech, came after her father Krok died without a male heir and the Czechs agreed to accept whoever she chose as husband. Her vision here foretold a farmer ploughing with two oxen at a particular spot on the river Belina beyond the hills: Premysl, who became her husband and founded the ruling dynasty. A small settlement and Prague's second castle stand here now. The aura is not given.

neighbours.name: The Boii Springs
neighbours.summary: Twelve hot mineral springs in the hills of western Bohemia beside the remains of a Celtic settlement, the largest a geyser forty feet high, pouring out so much hot water that the river Tepla runs warm for miles. Drinking the water cures ailments of the stomach. They are named for the Celtic Boii, from whom Bohemia takes its name. The aura is not given.

neighbours.name: Mount Blanik
neighbours.summary: A mountain of Bohemia covered by a Divine regio whose strength is not given. Where springs rise on its slopes an arch-shaped opening leads to a vast pillared hall underground where the Knights of Blanik, the sleeping army of St Wenceslaus (Divine, Might not given), sit at stone tables with their horses asleep beside them and their arms hung on the columns. Wenceslaus, Bohemia's patron and former duke, was murdered by his pagan brother Boleslav in the early tenth century; the prophecy says that in the Czechs' direst need he will rise, take the legendary sword of Bruncvik and come to Blanik to wake his army.

details.tethers: The sleeping army of St Wenceslaus

levels.name: The hall of the sleeping knights
levels.notes: A vast pillared underground hall (the regio's level and aura are not given). Weapons and armour hang on the columns, hundreds of horses stand asleep along one side, and their owners, the Knights of Blanik (Divine, Might not given), sit at stone tables in stone chairs.

neighbours.name: The Bohemian Forest
neighbours.summary: The mountain spine along Bohemia's border, a forest nearly as large as the Black Forest and kept free of people by its harsh climate and its many peat bogs, swamps and marshes. The north is open beech woodland; on the lower mountain slopes beech and chestnut give way to birch and evergreens; the south, in the rain-shadow of the Alps, holds most of the standing water, with willow and alder among the pines and stunted rotting trees that give it a sinister air; the drier western mountains carry ordinary woodland and then pine and fir higher up. Lynx, wolves and deer live here, and giants (realm and Might not given) haunt it. The forest's powers and personality are left to the storyguide and its aura is not given.

neighbours.name: The woods of Irencillia
neighbours.summary:
Beech and oak woodland in the northern Bohemian Forest where it meets the Bohemian plain, near the Maddenhofen Woods, with fallow deer, boar, lynx and bears common and few wolves, where the domus magna of House Merinita hides. The Faerie aura is highly patchy: at least 1 everywhere within the boundary, up to 6 where the sancta are sited, and odd spots run high (a covered walkway to the kitchens is Faerie 4 along its length); some high patches lie in small fragmented regiones with marked entrances. The theory is that the scattered aura and regiones are the fallout of a vast magical outpouring, the war between Quendalon and Myanar. The covenant appears differently to every visitor according to expectation, a faerie castle of living wood, a foresters' hamlet, a wooded hill with a trilithon over a labyrinth, a gully of caves, and those who do not know of it see only open woodland and wander through unknowingly; common to every view are an enclosing boundary, one gateway, and over it the inscription said to be Merinita's last words before she vanished in 785. Pieces taken out of the aura turn to dust, dry leaves and twigs at sunrise or sunset, and no usable map can be made. The surrounding land is kept wild by the covenant's meddling.

Secrets
Irencillia was never Merinita's home. Her true first domus magna, the temple of Diana of which she was the last Roman priestess, is lost and its name forgotten.

levels.name: The fragmented regiones
levels.see: Each entrance is marked with a symbol, a badger's head, a crescent moon and the like, whose meaning outsiders do not grasp
levels.notes: Scattered patches of high aura, most of the magi's sancta among them, each a small regio of its own; the aura within runs up to 6, and the levels are not numbered.

neighbours.name: Obri Hrad
neighbours.summary: The Giants' Castle, the remains of a primeval Celtic hill-fort on a hilltop above the river Losenice at the southern edge of the Bohemian Forest, strewn with great broken rocks the giants gathered. Its Magic aura of 3 makes it a possible covenant site, though the forest's giants (realm and Might not given) may still come by.

neighbours.name: The Maddenhofen Woods
neighbours.summary: House Merinita's name for a stretch of woods on the north-western fringe of the Bohemian Forest near Irencillia, which the covenant guards closely though it apparently takes no vis from them. Here the Founder Tytalus vanished in 807, declaring he would confront the Queen of all the Fae. The Merinita scoff at such a Queen, yet a powerful faerie (Faerie, Might not given) does live here who grants a petitioner's Heart's Desire in exchange for a task to be done afterwards, and nobody has ever completed one. The woods have a Stasis power, and Tytalus himself may be preserved within them. The aura is not given.

details.tethers: The faerie who grants the Heart's Desire

neighbours.name: The Margravate of Moravia
neighbours.summary: Bohemia's eastern March, bordered to the east by the Carpathians and Hungary, and so by the Transylvanian Tribunal; the river Morava runs through it to join the Danube in Austria. Its margrave is usually the Bohemian king's son or brother. It was part of Poland under Boleslaus I from 999 and has been part of Bohemia since 1019. Brünn is its seat, where the stuffed carcass of the dragon a travelling butcher killed with a hide full of unslaked lime hangs in the town hall. The aura is not given.

neighbours.name: The valley of Roznov
neighbours.summary:
A valley at the edge of the Carpathians on the Hungarian border in the extreme east of Moravia, under Mount Radhost, whose summit stands 3,700 feet high; a Magic aura of 4 covers the whole valley. A fort and village at the foot of the mountain control the single pass and trail up, and two-thirds of the way up a small twin-towered castle inside a curtain wall can be seen only from its own valley.

Secrets
Castle and fort are linked by tunnels through the mountain.

neighbours.name: The temple on Mount Radhost
neighbours.summary:
A crude stone temple on the summit of Mount Radhost with a Magic aura of 6. The mountain has always been sacred to Radegast, the Slavic god of chieftainship and war, fertility and harvest, and every summer solstice the whole covenant of Roznov and its village climb to celebrate him here with orgiastic drinking and debauchery, from which dozens of pawns of vis are harvested.

Secrets
A few celebrants are quietly seized each year and sacrificed inside the temple, seen only by the high priest Igor Rastvan's most loyal servants; the victims usually come from the covenant's slaves, their blood yields Corpus vis and fuels the harvest. It is never discussed, though most covenfolk guess why people vanish each summer, and some supernatural agency seems to keep it secret from the Tremere of the fort.

details.tethers: Radegast, whose sacred mountain this has always been

neighbours.name: Emperor Frederick II
neighbours.summary:
Holy Roman Emperor, the head of the Hohenstaufen house: born in 1194 to the emperor Henry VI and a Sicilian mother, made king of Germany in 1212, crowned at Aachen in 1214 and crowned emperor in Rome in 1220. He is also King of Sicily and bears the titles of King of Italy and of Burgundy. He keeps his court in Sicily, prefers it to Germany, and is expected to stay away from the kingdom for more than ten years.

A scholar and poet in the Sicilian tongue, author of a treatise on falconry and called the wonder of the world, he is tolerant of Moslems and of magic and has taken the hedge wizard Michael Scot into his court as his magician, which the Church holds against him. He swore to go on crusade and has made no move to do so, to the Pope's growing anger. At the Diet of Frankfurt in 1220 he granted customs privileges. His policy of clearing forest for settlement makes him an enemy of Dankmar.

neighbours.name: The Welfs of Brunswick
neighbours.summary:
The Saxon ducal house, rivals of the Hohenstaufen since the Swabians raised an anti-king against them in 1127; the book also gives the Welf name to the Ottonian emperors. Henry the Lion, duke of Saxony and the great opponent of Frederick Barbarossa, seized Lübeck in 1157 and made it a city; in 1180 his duchy was broken up, his lands given to Hohenstaufen supporters and Bavaria to Otto of Wittelsbach, and he was sent into exile.

His descendant Otto IV of Brunswick was elected rival king in 1198, crowned emperor in 1209, excommunicated in 1210, beaten at Bouvines in 1214 and died in 1218, leaving the house out of the crown.

neighbours.name: Count Palatine of the Rhine (Wittelsbach)
neighbours.summary:
The Wittelsbach dukes of Bavaria, who have lately gained the County Palatine of the Rhine, the lands about the Palatinate Forest and the Odenwald. A count palatine began as the judicial governor of a royal estate, an office made to balance the dukes; it is now hereditary.

Barbarossa gave Bavaria, the old Welf stronghold, to Otto of Wittelsbach after Henry the Lion's fall in 1180. A later Otto of Wittelsbach, count palatine, murdered King Philip of Swabia at Bamberg in 1208.

neighbours.name: Dukes of Upper Lorraine
neighbours.summary: The dukes rule Upper Lorraine from the fortress Duke Gerard raised at Nancy, hemmed in between the kings of France and the rival counts of Bar and Luxemburg. They have never recovered Metz, whose burghers threw them out in 1143 and now thwart them at every turn, though Toul stays loyal. Duke Dietrich III is expected to die this year, 1220, and his heir Matthew II to succeed him.

neighbours.name: Counts of Holland
neighbours.summary: The counts are draining new land from the marshes of the Rhine delta and founding towns on it, and with the bishop of Utrecht they hunt the pirates of the Zuider Sea, a fight centred on Deventer.

neighbours.name: Dukes of Brabant
neighbours.summary: Lower Lorraine has broken into two rival duchies, Brabant and Limburg, with small counties filling the rest; Brabant is the greater. The lords of Cleves ruled Brabant once but do so no longer.

neighbours.name: Dukes of Limburg
neighbours.summary: The second of the two principal duchies into which Lower Lorraine has split, in rivalry with Brabant; the rest of the old duchy is a scatter of small counties.

neighbours.name: Lords of Cleves
neighbours.summary: The lords hold the Schwanenburg, the Swan Castle above Cleves on the lower Rhine, and bear a swan in their arms. They once ruled Brabant but have lost it.

neighbours.name: The Zähringens
neighbours.summary:
Former dukes of Swabia whose estates lay in the fertile strip between the Rhine and the Black Forest. In the twelfth century they were the foremost castle builders of western Swabia and drew power and taxes from the Black Forest monasteries they founded and controlled. Conrad Zähringen founded Freiburg in 1120; the family castle stands just north of the town, and a lesser branch has its seat in the lower town of Baden.

The main line failed in 1218 and the Hohenstaufen have taken much of its land. Their settlement of the forest cost Durenmar several magical sites early in the twelfth century; some wonder whether the covenant patronised the house or caused its withering, which is thought unlikely.

neighbours.name: The Hohenstaufens
neighbours.summary: The imperial dynasty of Conrad III, Frederick Barbarossa and the present emperor Frederick II, and the Zähringens' rivals for Swabia, where they now hold much of the failed house's land. Their ancestral castle crowns the Hohenstaufen hill, the grandest of the three Kaiserberge south of Gmünd, the town Conrad III founded. The emperor's policy of clearing forest makes the house an enemy of Dankmar.

neighbours.name: The Hohenzollerns
neighbours.summary: Local lords of the Swabian Jura who have built forts on the defensible limestone peaks of those harsh hills.

neighbours.name: The Free Imperial Cities
neighbours.summary:
Fourteen cities that in 1220 owe allegiance only to the emperor, who frees rich towns so their wealth is denied to rival dukes: Dortmund, Esslingen, Goslar, Hamburg, Metz, Nördlingen, Nuremberg, Regensburg, Schwäbisch-Hall, Speyer, Ulm, Wetzlar, Wimpfen and Worms. Ulm was freed in 1155 (the Black Forest chapter gives 1164), Hamburg in 1189 and Nuremberg in 1219.

Lübeck is expected to join them in 1226, Aachen and Erfurt in 1250 and Cologne not until 1288.

details.rules: Each city answers to the emperor alone and not to any local lord; several are governed by their own councils.
details.wants: Trade unhindered by any lord's tolls or wars.
details.offers: Wealth kept out of the hands of rival dukes, and loyalty to the crown.

neighbours.name: The Teutonic Knights
neighbours.summary: The Order of Teutonic Knights, founded at Acre in 1190, crusades against the pagans of the Baltic alongside the Livonian Order of the Knights of the Sword, formed in 1202 in Pomerania and Livonia. The Sword Brothers are expected to be reprimanded and absorbed into the Teutonic Order in 1237, and the Order to conquer Prussia in 1240.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Mainz
neighbours.summary:
The first churchman of Germany: Archchancellor of the Empire, chief of the princes who elect the king, the prelate who crowns him at Aachen, and as primate of Germany the Pope's deputy north of the Alps. His see counts as a Holy See, the only one besides Rome, which gives the cathedral its Divine aura of 7. The line began with St Boniface in the eighth century, and Willigis won the Archchancellorship in the tenth.

Rhine traffic transships at Mainz for the Main and the upper river, and the customs make the archbishop very rich. The episcopal palace saw the ritual suicide of the city's Jews in 1096. The book does not name the present archbishop or give his stance toward magi; the Peace of Mainz is expected to be proclaimed here in 1235.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Cologne
neighbours.summary:
Archchancellor of Italy, a prince of the Empire and ruler of its greatest city, which holds the relics of the Three Magi that Frederick Barbarossa carried off from Milan in 1164. The present archbishop, Engelbert I, is tall, fair and just, praised by the poet Walther von der Vogelweide; if history holds he will be murdered in 1225.

His stance toward magi is not given, though Fengheld keeps a chapter house in his city. Cologne is expected to become a Free Imperial City only in 1288.

neighbours.name: Archbishop of Trier
neighbours.summary:
The third of the great Rhenish prince-archbishops, lord of the oldest city in Germany and its oldest church, the cathedral of St Peter. In 1200 the archbishop led an army of angry townsfolk that destroyed the covenant of Rheinstein in the Rhine Gorge, after which the Tribunal banned magic in the Gorge for twenty years: a hostile precedent toward magi.

Trier's earlier covenant, Treverorum, had already been fined and then collapsed between 1165 and 1172 over its meddling with the town and the Church.

neighbours.name: Prince-bishop of Worms
neighbours.summary: The bishop rules Worms in his own right as a prince of the Empire, holding a royal fief of the kind earlier kings granted bishops to counter the dukes and governing through a lay advocate with power of life and death. His cathedral has a Divine aura of 6. His stance toward magi is not given.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Speyer
neighbours.summary: The bishop rules Speyer, the Salian emperors' favourite seat, whose cathedral (Divine aura 6) was begun by Conrad II in 1030 and holds kings and emperors in its crypt. During the First Crusade massacre his protection saved most of the city's Jews, though a dozen were killed in the cathedral for refusing baptism.

neighbours.name: Prince-bishop of Liège
neighbours.summary: Liège has been a prince-bishopric since Otto II granted the diocese as a fief to Bishop Notger, who built the cathedral of St Lambert, the bishops' palace and the walls. The see has outgrown Verdun. Henry IV died here excommunicate.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Utrecht
neighbours.summary: An early missionary bishopric of the Rhine delta. The bishop holds estates in the lands the counts of Holland are draining, and with the counts fights the pirates of the Zuider Sea.

neighbours.name: Convent of St Odile (Hohenburg)
neighbours.summary: A pilgrimage convent on Mount Saint Odile in the Vosges, where the saint was buried in 720; its spring has a Divine aura of 4.

neighbours.name: Hirsau
neighbours.summary:
Probably the most powerful monastery in Germany, by a bridge over the Nagold north-east of the Black Forest, some fifteen miles north of Durenmar. Founded in 1059 with the relics of St Aurelius, a fifth-century Armenian bishop, it now has more than a hundred monks and daughter houses all over Germany, St Georgen among them. It led the eleventh-century Hirsau reform that freed religious houses from lay lords and bishops, bringing the customs of Cluny into Germany. Built of red sandstone, its basilica of St Aurelius is a hundred yards long.

Its Divine aura is 5, and whether from the aura, its size or its place at the forest's edge it is largely immune to the faerie attacks other Black Forest houses suffer. It spreads rumours of Durenmar as a hidden city of sorcerers; magi for their part note how alike the two are, each a learned centre with many daughter houses holding back the forest. Legend has it that a Bonisagus archmagus renounced magic, took orders and helped found the house, and some think the monastery may be heir to his magical legacy, though no magus has braved the Dominion to find out.

neighbours.name: Gengenbach
neighbours.summary: A monastery at the western end of the long uninhabited stretch of the Black Forest Road; the book gives no more about it.

neighbours.name: Kloster Blaubeuren
neighbours.summary: A monastery beside the Blautopf pool at the southern edge of the Swabian Jura, whose humble monks go to the water faerie called the Schöne Lau to have their futures told.

neighbours.name: Zweifalten
neighbours.summary: A monastery on the south side of the Swabian Jura, near the Wimsener Höhle where the River Ach runs underground; the book gives no more about it.

neighbours.name: Cologne
neighbours.summary:
The largest and grandest city in Germany and the biggest in the Empire north of the Alps, with more than twenty thousand citizens: the chief trading town of the kingdom and the hub of the Rhine. Roman Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensis, settled in 38 BC and a colony from 50 AD at Agrippina's request, it was capital of Lower Germania; Constantine's bridge of 310 has long since fallen. Walls of 1180 with a dozen gates and a moat enclose a half-circle two miles across on the west bank; sixteen great churches stand beside the cathedral (Divine aura 6), with many chapels and monasteries, and a quayside more than a mile long holds hundreds of ships with the main market behind it. Its weavers, dyers, goldsmiths, weaponsmiths and armourers are famous.

The archbishop rules the city. The bones of the Three Magi, taken from Milan in 1164, lie in a golden shrine in the cathedral, and the church of St Ursula stands where the princess and her eleven thousand and ten virgins were slain by the Huns. The city's banner shows a two-headed black eagle with sword and sceptre under an archbishop's crown, with three gold crowns for the Magi and eleven flames for Ursula's thousands on its breast. The Jews were massacred here in 1096 and again in 1147. Fengheld keeps a chapter house in the Rheingasse near the market, staffed by Apple Gild magi. A vast new cathedral is expected to be begun in 1248, and the city to become a Free Imperial City in 1288.

neighbours.name: Mainz
neighbours.summary:
Roman Moguntiacum, founded in 13 BC, on the Rhine where the Main comes in; an archbishopric since St Boniface in the eighth century and the Church's centre for all Germany. Its red sandstone cathedral has six towers and two choirs, one for the clergy and one for the emperor, and like St Peter's runs east to west; hemmed in by buildings, among them St Gothard, the archbishop's chapel, it has a Divine aura of 7 as a Holy See.

Goods bound for Frankfurt on the Main or the upper Rhine are transshipped here, and the customs make the archbishop very rich. The Jewish academy has been famous since the tenth century, drawing students from Spain and Italy; the Jews of the city died by their own hands in the episcopal palace in 1096 and suffered again in 1147.

The seat of Archbishop Siegfried II, Archchancellor of the Empire, who takes its customs duties; home of the famous Jewish academy; the last stop on the road from Frankfurt to the Gorge. If the book's future holds, Mainz and Worms found the Rhine League in the 1250s.

neighbours.name: Trier
neighbours.summary:
On the Mosel; Roman Augusta Treverorum, founded in 16 BC on an older settlement and the oldest city in Germany. Constantine made it the western capital of the empire between 306 and 337, and its cathedral of St Peter is Germany's oldest church. The archbishop's seat; in 1096 the city's Jews drowned themselves rather than accept baptism. The covenant of Treverorum stood here until it was abolished in 1172.

The oldest city in Germany, named for the Celtic Treverii, raised by Augustus to a regional capital and under Constantine the capital of the western Empire with more than eighty thousand people; now barely a tenth of that live within smaller walls inside the Roman footprint, among the most complete Roman remains in Germany above, outside and beneath the city. Archbishop Dietrich I rules it and takes its customs duties. Wine is the chief export, shipped down to Koblenz.

Its landmarks: Constantine's Basilica, a brick throne hall eighty yards long that is now the archbishop's palace; the cathedral of St Peter, the oldest church in Germany and one of Constantine's four founding churches with St Peter's in Rome, the Holy Sepulchre and the Nativity, on ground given by his mother St Helena and keeping the Seamless Robe Christ wore at the crucifixion; the Porta Nigra, a four-storey Roman gate of sandstone in the north wall made the church of St Simeon in 1035 for a Greek hermit saint, with the Simeonstift beside it; the Kaiserthermen rebuilt as a castle in the south-east wall; the ruined Barbarathermen outside the walls; the Frankenturm merchant tower; the basilica of St Matthias just south, with the apostle's bones brought by St Helena; and the amphitheatre on the Hermesstrasse. The city has a Jewish community, David ben David its most prominent merchant, though the famous Jewish academy is at Mainz.

Trier is no friend to magi: its churchmen drove out Treverorum in 1172, and its archbishop led the army that destroyed Rheinstein in 1200.

neighbours.name: Worms
neighbours.summary:
An Upper Rhine city of Celts, Romans, Burgundians and Franks, a Free Imperial City ruled by its own prince-bishop. The Burgundians made it their capital in 413 and the Nibelungenlied is set here; Charlemagne and Barbarossa married here, and the Concordat of 1122 that ended the Investiture Contest was sealed here. The squat cathedral (Divine aura 6), with two domed choirs, four round towers of seven tiers and strange statues, stands on the old Burgundian castle Charlemagne made his palace; an inscription calls it the Romans' holy temple, the Nibelungs' fortress and Charlemagne's hall, and its north door, the Kaiserportal, marks the quarrel of the queens Kriemhild and Brünhild.

The northern third of the city is Little Jerusalem, the largest Jewish settlement in Germany, sacked in the first two Crusades; its synagogue was finished in 1175 and its ancient cemetery, the Heiliger Sand, lies outside the west wall. Frederick II is expected to wed Elizabeth of England here in 1235.

neighbours.name: Speyer
neighbours.summary:
A Roman camp on the Upper Rhine that became the favourite seat of the Salian emperors in the early eleventh century, and a Free Imperial City ruled by its bishop. Conrad II began the great cathedral in 1030 (Divine aura 6); kings and emperors lie in its crypt. The wealthy Jewish quarter south-west of the cathedral has a grand synagogue and bath-houses and trains rabbis; the bishop's protection saved most of its people in the First Crusade massacre, though a dozen were murdered in the cathedral for refusing baptism, and the city suffered again in 1147.

The bells of Speyer ring of themselves when an emperor dies. They stayed silent for the excommunicated Henry IV until his body was reburied here five years on and his faithful servant Kurt died, and for Henry V they rang the pattern tolled for a sinner led to execution.

neighbours.name: Strassburg
neighbours.summary: Roman Argentoratum, on a Celtic fishing village where the Ill meets the Upper Rhine; wrecked several times by invaders, it is now a thriving trading city at a crossroads, its name meaning the castle of roads, and is built around canals. The powerful boatmen's gild controls much of the trade of the Upper Rhine. Its ruler is not given.

neighbours.name: Basel
neighbours.summary: On the Upper Rhine where the river turns north, at the head of navigation. House Mercere keeps the Copper Rooster Inn here for Redcaps passing between the Greater Alps, Rhine and Normandy Tribunals. Its ruler is not given.

neighbours.name: Mulhouse
neighbours.summary: A town of the southern Vosges and Upper Rhine, a dozen miles east of Thann Chapel; the book says no more of it.

neighbours.name: Metz
neighbours.summary: Gaulish and then Roman Divodurum, where the Seille joins the Mosel in Upper Lorraine; sacked by the Huns, when St Livier, beheaded by Attila, carried his head to his hilltop grave. Capital of Austrasia in the sixth century and of Lotharingia in the ninth. A Free Imperial City since its burghers rose against the duke in 1143, it is now a rich little republic behind stern walls that lends money to the French king, the Emperor and the dukes, and keeps thwarting the dukes of Upper Lorraine. Its cathedral of St Stephen is one of several grand churches.

neighbours.name: Toul
neighbours.summary: Roman Tullum, forty miles up the Mosel from Metz: venerable but poorer and with fewer tales to tell, loyal to the duke of Upper Lorraine, behind tall white stone walls that are partly Roman.

neighbours.name: Verdun
neighbours.summary: On the Meuse above the Ardennes in Upper Lorraine; the treaty that divided the Carolingian empire was made here in 843, and the Treaty of Mersen of 870 passed it to the western kingdom before it came into the Empire. A border city of intrigue that grew in the eleventh century and now declines behind Liège and Metz; spies and assassins can be hired here for work on either side of the border. Redcaps often meet here on the way between the Rhine and Normandy Tribunals.

neighbours.name: Nancy
neighbours.summary: The seat of the dukes of Upper Lorraine, grown round the fortress Duke Gerard built between two marshes in the eleventh century as the central stronghold of his duchy.

neighbours.name: Xanten
neighbours.summary: On the west bank of the lower Rhine: Roman Colonia Ulpia Traiana, where St Victor and the Theban Legion were martyred; the new town grew on their graveyard as Ad Sanctos Martyres, shortened to Xanten. The birthplace of Siegfried, the old capital of the Nibelungs' land and the first home of the Rhinegold. Its ruler is not given.

neighbours.name: Cleves
neighbours.summary: A lower Rhine town below the Schwanenburg, held by the lords of Cleves, who bear a swan in their arms and no longer rule Brabant.

neighbours.name: Deventer
neighbours.summary: A modest town on the right bank of the lower Rhine, set in marshland with waterways to the Zuider Sea and the river mouths, and with Utrecht one of the early missionary bishoprics. Its church of St Lebuinus began as a chapel in 768, was burnt by the Saxons and rebuilt by St Liudger in 776. It is the centre of the war the counts of Holland and the bishop of Utrecht wage on the Zuider Sea pirates; the town militia hunts them, yet sailors of doubtful character can still be hired here.

neighbours.name: Aachen
neighbours.summary:
Charlemagne's palace city in Lower Lorraine, on the road from Cologne to Liège and Flanders. He founded it in 768 after his horse stepped into a hot sulphur spring beside Roman baths, raised a round church shaped like a hoof over it, held his court here and was buried here in 814. German kings are crowned here by the archbishop of Mainz, on his throne of marble, wood and gold at the top of six steps: Otto I in 936 and Frederick II in 1214.

No longer of political weight, the city keeps a cathedral (Divine aura 6) with a matchless hoard of relics, among them John the Baptist's garments, the Virgin's gown and Christ's swaddling clothes, and a newly finished shrine over Charlemagne's tomb. It is expected to become a Free Imperial City in 1250.

neighbours.name: Liège
neighbours.summary: A sizeable market city of Lower Lorraine where the Legia joins the Meuse, grown round the miracle-working tomb St Hubert raised for the martyred St Lambert, bishop of Tongeren, in the seventh century. Otto II granted the diocese to Bishop Notger as a fief, and he built the cathedral of St Lambert, the prince-bishops' palace and the walls. Henry IV died here excommunicate.

neighbours.name: Utrecht
neighbours.summary: An early missionary bishopric in the Rhine delta. Its bishop holds estates in the draining lands of Holland and fights the Zuider Sea pirates together with the counts of Holland.

neighbours.name: Baden
neighbours.summary: Roman Aquae, between the Rhine valley and the north-western slopes of the Black Forest, named for the hot springs halfway up the Florentinerberg that cure rheumatism and arthritis; the Romans built extensive baths. The upper town is mostly ruined and keeps a Magic aura of 2; Durenmar claims it as Hermetic property and harvests vis from the springs. The lower town is the seat of a lesser Zähringen branch. Not the other spa called Baden a hundred miles south beyond the Rhine, in the Greater Alps Tribunal.
neighbours.ruler: A lesser branch of the Zähringens

neighbours.name: Freiburg
neighbours.summary: The largest settlement about the Black Forest, founded in 1120 by Conrad Zähringen in the valley of the Dreisam with wooded heights on three sides. Around 1200 its citizens began paying for a lofty cathedral of the local red sandstone. The Zähringen castle stands a short way to the north.

neighbours.name: Rottweil
neighbours.summary:
On the eastern edge of the forest at the eastern end of the Black Forest Road, perched defensibly over the upper Neckar. Roman Arae Flaviae, the Altar of the Flavians, was meant as a provincial capital at a crossroads until the frontier moved on; Roman temples, baths and buildings lie buried under the town, fewer than at Baden.

Home of the Rottweiler, a large, fierce black-and-tan dog bred from Roman stock crossed with the dark faerie dogs of the forest, called the butcher's dog because butchers train it to pull carts; it seldom barks, keeps poor guard and attacks superbly. At least one Rhine magus keeps Rottweilers in place of grogs; a strongly faerie-blooded one ages like a man and often has Second Sight or Faerie Blood, while an ordinary dog makes seven aging rolls a year.

neighbours.name: Offenburg
neighbours.summary: The town at the western end of the Black Forest Road; the book gives no more about it.

neighbours.name: Waldmössingen
neighbours.summary: An isolated village on the site of a ruined Roman fort at the eastern end of the Black Forest Road's uninhabited thirty-mile stretch.

neighbours.name: Gmünd
neighbours.summary: A town of the Stauferland, the rolling hills between the Swabian Forest and the Swabian Jura named for the Hohenstaufens, founded by Conrad III in the twelfth century on the line of the Roman limes. It makes luxuries, jewellery and glassware. South of it rise the three round wooded Kaiserberge, each topped by a castle: Hohenstaufen to the west, the lowest and grandest and the imperial ancestral seat, Hohenrechberg, and Stuifen to the east, the highest.

neighbours.name: Ulm
neighbours.summary: On the north bank of the upper Danube, first settled in the ninth century by Jews, of whom a small community remains. Frederick Barbarossa made it a Free Imperial City in 1164 and it has grown prosperous since: flax fields surround it, its many weavers make linen, and the cloth is traded across the Empire.

neighbours.name: Seebach
neighbours.summary: A settlement in the mountains near Mummel Lake, whose nixe comes down to the villages round about to bewitch young men.

neighbours.name: Jewish academy of Mainz
neighbours.summary: The centre of Jewish scholarship in Germany since the tenth century, known across Europe and drawing students from Spain and Italy. It gave rise to the Chasidic renaissance and to reforms of the law that widened women's rights and permitted usury, so that pious Jews could trade.

neighbours.name: Bjornaer and Merinita, guides of the forest paths
neighbours.summary: The only two Houses that can show a seeker the paths through the forest: the heartbeast mystery of House Bjornaer is itself a path that every apprentice walks, and some Merinita know the routes into Arcadia. Their methods are alien to one another and to House Bonisagus; Causabon of Bonisagus muses that the three domus magnae each hold a fragment of the truth and ought to pool their secrets.

details.offers: A guide to the paths of power through the forest, for those who can follow.

neighbours.name: The Hercynius lineage of House Bonisagus
neighbours.summary:
A rumour from Causabon's journal: that a remaining few who follow Hercynius are working to channel the primal magic of the forests and finish the opus maximum of Bonisagus, who believed that Hermetic magic was only the beginning of it.

Secrets
The lineage's existence and purpose are rumour only; the book confirms nothing.

details.wants: To channel the forests' primal magic and complete the great work Bonisagus began.

neighbours.name: Hedge wizards of the forest paths
neighbours.summary: Some hedge wizards know the paths of power through the forests and will teach them to magi for the right price. Mundanes who yield themselves to the forest gain minor spells and commonly end up possessed, serving as the spirit's agents beyond the trees.

details.offers: Teaching of a path through the forest to magi, for a suitable price.

neighbours.name: Forest Guardians
neighbours.summary: Rhine magi, most of them Bjornaer, who publicly claim a wilderness as their Hermetic territory and defend it. The Rhine Peripheral Code encourages magi to defend wild places, which gives them some standing and little else in law. Becoming a Guardian is a sacrifice to the forest's spirit, and Guardians are rarely seen at Tribunal afterwards.

details.rules: A Guardian publicly declares a wilderness his Hermetic territory and defends it; the Rhine Peripheral Code encourages the defence of wildernesses but gives him little other legal footing.
details.wants: To keep the forests they guard untouched.

neighbours.name: The Brethren of the Free Spirit
neighbours.summary:
A heretical pantheist cult born of Paris theologians at the start of the thirteenth century, from David of Dinant's teaching that God, matter and mind are one substance; it has spread in secret to Cologne and the country round it, among commoners and among nobles who want lordship free of the Church. Since all is God, nothing is sin: the Brethren hold naked masses to recreate Eden and indulge in licence and crime, and their fanatics claim that fire and torture cannot harm them. They herald a new age of the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Vehm of Saxony counts them mortal enemies, hunts them and means to prove their claims false.

Secrets
An option for the saga: the magi of Fengheld's Cologne chapter house, all of the Apple Gild, may lead the Brethren, and a part of the cult may be a Mystery Cult of Rhine and Normandy magi; the creed suits the Apple Gild's aim of winning mundane acceptance of magic.

details.rules: If all is God, nothing is sin.
details.wants: A new age of the Holy Spirit, and for its noble members lordship free of the Church.
details.offers: Indulgence without sin, and for fanatics a claimed immunity to fire and torture.

neighbours.name: The Chasidim
neighbours.summary: The German Jewish pietists, a mystical movement that arose after the First Crusade and centres on the academy of Mainz. They teach asceticism, martyrdom and lifelong penitence, and have reformed the law to widen women's rights and to permit usury, so that pious Jews may trade.

details.rules: Asceticism, readiness for martyrdom and lifelong penitence.

neighbours.name: Boatmen's gild of Strassburg
neighbours.summary: A powerful gild that controls much of the trade of the Upper Rhine from the canals of Strassburg.

details.wants: Its hold on the river trade of the Upper Rhine.
details.offers: Passage and carriage on the Upper Rhine.

neighbours.name: Zuider Sea pirates
neighbours.summary: Pirates who roam the inland sea off Deventer. The town's militia, the counts of Holland and the bishop of Utrecht all hunt them, yet disreputable sailors still hire out in Deventer.

details.offers: Sailors of doubtful character for hire in Deventer.

neighbours.name: The Cult of Mercury
neighbours.summary: The Roman magician-priests of the Rhine frontier towns, long gone. They sensed the power of the Hercynian forest spirit, built a temple on the site where Durenmar now stands and there bound the Black Forest's spirit by oath into the Fane of the Founders, guided the legions' limes and the Black Forest Road with warding milestones, and linked their temples and roads by magic into a barrier against the wilderness of Germania Magna. In doing so they began the great spirit's fragmentation; the splinter they bound later became the King of the Black Mountain.

neighbours.name: Bockmen
neighbours.summary:
Goat-headed, goat-legged faeries of Might 20 (Animal) and Size -1 with backward-curving horns, feral eyes and slavering jaws, who lurk by the paths of the Black Forest and the oldest German forests, nearly always alone. Invisible while still, they unsettle travellers and their mounts for hours (birds fall silent, dread grows, brave traits sink by one each hour, and no one sleeps or recovers fatigue), then leap out to strike with fear that sends the victim fleeing until exhausted or collapsing until dawn. They are weak and cowardly in a fight (claws Init +9, Attack +13, Defence +9, Damage +3; Soak +5; iron does them two extra damage) but succeed in their purpose, which is to keep people out of the forest.

Orphedra of Dankmar has a pact with the local bockmen to patrol the surroundings of her covenant.

details.rules: Nearly always alone; discourage travel through the forest.
details.offers: A pawn of Animal vis in the right horn and one of Mentem in the left.

neighbours.name: Dark fae of the deep Black Forest
neighbours.summary: The most malign faeries of the Black Forest haunt its deepest parts, furthest from people; many are shapeless or formless, embodying darkness, fear and malice, and they are the cause of the panic mortals feel in wild places. Several dark courts exist, all under the King of the Black Mountain. Dankmar deals with them carefully; Durenmar has known nothing of them since the Hercynian lineage was exiled.
neighbours.ruler: The King of the Black Mountain

details.wants: An end to all human intrusion into the deep forest.

neighbours.name: Schwall of Bjornaer and the Rhine elemental
neighbours.summary:
An elderly Bjornaer of the Hawthorn Gild, once of Rheinstein, lives alone at the Rhinefalls. Odd disturbances of the river would be the first sign that something is wrong.

Secrets
Schwall, a powerful Wilderist hidden in the Rhinefalls regio, means to release the imprisoned spirit of the Rhine and merge with it to cheat Final Twilight. The floods would devastate shipping, towns and cities the length of the river, a breach of the Code the Tribunal would answer with a Wizard's March. Magi may hinder him or help him.

stages.title: Disturbances on the river
stages.clues: Unexplained surges, eddies and floods along the Rhine.
stages.ignored: Schwall's preparations go on unseen in the regio.
stages.stopped: A search of the Rhinefalls regio finds the old magus.

stages.title: The elemental released
stages.clues: The falls change; the river rises out of season.
stages.ignored: Floods devastate shipping, towns and cities down the whole Rhine; the Tribunal calls a March.
stages.stopped: The spirit stays bound and Schwall faces his Twilight.
stages.turned: Magi who help him share in whatever he becomes.

neighbours.name: The forest spirits' wrath
neighbours.summary: Wholesale or repeated magical harm to a forest draws the attention of its spirit. It can grant Flaws, possess, shroud a place, drown a region in grown undergrowth, turn the weather or drive beasts as puppets, and its Might of 30 or more resists the magic used against it.

stages.title: The spirit takes notice
stages.clues: Beasts watch the offenders; paths close; the weather turns.
stages.ignored: The spirit acts against the covenant.
stages.stopped: Amends made to the forest, and the harm not repeated.

stages.title: Reprisal
stages.ignored: Flaws granted, people possessed, the covenant shrouded or swallowed in undergrowth, storms and driven beasts.

neighbours.name: Walking the paths
neighbours.summary: Hermetic training does not cover the primal power of the forest. Those who walk its paths are scarred in body and mind, take permanent Flaws as sacrifices, and often lose their way or are never seen again; a regio of stasis can swallow decades, as when Alexander of Jerbiton came back too late for his mater. The paths may explain the Rhine's long record of magi who quietly vanish or retire.

neighbours.name: Malicious woodland spirits
neighbours.summary: The Baumesel, the ass of the trees, and the bockman of the Black Forest attack lone travellers; the Eschenfrau, the wife of the ash, is very evil to her neighbours and must be appeased with a sacrifice on Ash Wednesday. The book gives no realm or Might for these three.

neighbours.name: Pulch of Merinita
neighbours.summary:
The folk of Thuringia take Pulch, who haunts the Kammerforst and punishes wood-thieves and those who harm the trees, for a spirit of the forest.

Secrets
He is a Merinita magus skirting the edge of the Code; Quaesitores may send characters to bring him to account.

neighbours.name: The Wild Hunt and the Holzfrau
neighbours.summary: A covenant in a wilderness, above all in a Faerie aura, may stand on the spot where the local wood-wife has always hidden from the Hunt. Every autumn she tries to get in, and on stormy winter nights the Wild Hunt assaults the covenant.

details.antagonist: The local wood-wife and the Wild Hunt

stages.title: The wood-wife comes
stages.clues: In autumn a Holzfrau of Might 20 seeks a way inside the covenant.
stages.ignored: She is kept out and the Hunt finds her in the open.
stages.turned: Sheltered, she repays the kindness; the Hunt comes looking.

stages.title: The Wild Hunt
stages.clues: Storms on winter nights, and horns in the wind.
stages.ignored: The Hunt assaults the covenant.

neighbours.name: Pogroms
neighbours.summary: Every announcement of a crusade sets off massacres of the Jews in the Rhine cities, as in 1096 at Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne and Trier and again around 1147. Only the bishops hanging the ringleaders brings them to a stop.

stages.title: A crusade is preached
stages.clues: Preachers and crusader bands gather in the Rhine cities.
stages.ignored: Mobs turn on the Jewish quarters.

stages.title: Massacre
stages.ignored: The Jewish quarters are sacked and their people killed.
stages.stopped: The bishop hangs the ringleaders and the killing ends.

neighbours.name: Verdun's underworld
neighbours.summary: In Verdun, a declining border city, spies and assassins can be hired to work in French or German lands by whoever pays.

neighbours.name: The destruction of St Georgen
neighbours.summary:
The Benedictine monastery of St Georgen, founded in 1084 as a small daughter house of Hirsau, was the Dominion's deepest incursion into the Black Forest and so the greatest threat to its ancient power; its bell was carried off to the Seven Waterfalls. The wilderness attacked it again and again, it was abandoned more than once and always refounded. In 1208 travellers found its buildings and fields in ruin, overgrown with strange dark vines in which the twisted bodies of the monks hung, their faces frozen in horror.

The Order suspected Dankmar. The matter was raised at the Tribunal of 1214, where Jiphella, Dankmar's only delegate, denied it; the deed would be lawful in the letter under the Guardians of the Forests ruling, though the Tribunal would never openly approve, and with no mundane witnesses there was no breach of the Code. A close vote refused an investigation.

Secrets
Dankmar's part in the destruction is suspected; the book does not state it as fact.

details.antagonist: The wilderness of the Black Forest; Dankmar suspected

stages.title: The monks found dead
stages.clues: Travellers find St Georgen in ruin, its monks hanging in dark vines.
stages.ignored: The Order suspects Dankmar; the house is not refounded.

stages.title: The Tribunal declines to investigate
stages.clues: Jiphella denies Dankmar's involvement; the vote is close.
stages.ignored: The suspicion stays unanswered and the forest's power grows.
stages.turned: A new case brought at the next Tribunal reopens the question.

neighbours.name: Monastery attacks by the King of the Black Mountain
neighbours.summary: The other monasteries of the Black Forest that lie inside the King of the Black Mountain's domain suffer sinister attacks and unexplained accidents: monks vanish, crops are blighted, and landslides and earthquakes strike. Hirsau alone is largely immune.

details.antagonist: The King of the Black Mountain

neighbours.name: Valdemar II of Denmark
neighbours.summary: King of Denmark, called the Victorious, and the overlord of the whole northern coast of the Tribunal. He took Holstein in 1201 and occupied Hamburg in 1216, and in 1214 Frederick II formally recognised his hold on Holstein and Pomerania in return for Danish support of his claim to the Empire. His father Valdemar I conquered Rügen in 1168 after secretly climbing the Königstuhl, and burnt Rostock in 1161 to drive out the pagans; it is not known whether the son has made the climb. Prince Mestwin of Pomerania has sworn allegiance to him, and he keeps an uneasy alliance with the Knights of the Sword. The coastal towns chafe under him and want Free Imperial City status; if history holds, Adolf IV of Holstein defeats him in 1227 and Holstein and Pomerania return to the Empire.

neighbours.name: Duke Erich of Holstein
neighbours.summary: A Dane of the house of Sven Estridson who governs Holstein as duke on behalf of King Valdemar II. Lübeck, Hamburg and Nortorf lie in his charge.

neighbours.name: Albert I, Duke of Saxony
neighbours.summary: The present duke of Saxony, of the Ascanian line descended from Albert the Bear, the rival of Henry the Lion who profited most when the great Welf fell. The Welfs remain the ancestral house of Saxony and the chief rivals of the ruling Hohenstaufen, so the duke's title sits uneasily on lands whose towns still remember Henry.

neighbours.name: The Princes of Mecklenburg
neighbours.summary:
A Sorbian dynasty named for their castle between Lübeck and Rostock, a little inland north of Schwerin, who rule Rostock. The family and the region once worshipped Radegast, until Valdemar I burnt Rostock in 1161 and drove the pagans into the countryside. They have since accepted Christianity and sworn to the emperor, hoping to win back their ancestral lands.

Secrets
The Mecklenburgs still secretly worship Radegast and have gained unnatural powers from him. Imanitos Mendax of Oculus Septentrionalis has lately appeared to them as a prophet of the god.

neighbours.name: Archbishop Gerhard II of Bremen
neighbours.summary: The oldest Saxon bishopric, founded in the eighth century when Charlemagne sent the missionary Willehad to the Saxons; the first church rose in 789 and a sizeable cathedral stands there now. The see moved here from Hamburg after the Wendish raids. St Ansgar, the Apostle of the North, lies buried here since 865. Archbishop Gerhard II contends with Bremen's independent-minded merchants for control of the city.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Corvey
neighbours.summary: A great scholarly abbey near Höxter, twenty miles east of Paderborn, where in the tenth century the monk Widukind wrote his history of the Saxons.

neighbours.name: Archbishopric of Magdeburg
neighbours.summary: Otto the Great founded a Benedictine monastery and the cathedral at Magdeburg and raised it to an archbishopric in 962. It has been the centre of missionary work and Church authority over the Eastern Marches ever since.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of St Liudger, Münster
neighbours.summary: Founded in 805 as a monastery, from which the city takes its name, to serve as a base for converting the Saxons. The cathedral is dedicated to St Liudger, its first bishop.

neighbours.name: Collegiate foundation of Quedlinburg
neighbours.summary: A foundation for noblewomen established by Mathilde, widow of Henry the Fowler. Its abbesses have ruled the town of Quedlinburg since.

neighbours.name: Schleswig
neighbours.summary: A fishing town on the north side of the Schlei fjord, grown up some two hundred years after the Vikings' Haithabu beside a Benedictine cloister of St Johannis. The earth ramparts and burial mounds of Haithabu, where the land crossing between the Baltic and the North Sea is shortest, lie a few miles off, and locals say its ghosts remain.

neighbours.name: Hamburg
neighbours.summary: A sizeable trading city on the Elbe estuary, founded early in the ninth century, destroyed by a Viking fleet in 845, burnt by the Poles in 1030 and raided twice by the Wends, after which its archbishop moved his see to Bremen. Frederick Barbarossa freed it of tax and customs on sea and river goods in 1189 and made it a Free Imperial City, but Valdemar II occupied it in 1216 and it now owes allegiance to Denmark. It controls the Lüneburg salt that Lübeck needs for its herring. If history holds, its free status returns in 1227.

neighbours.name: Nortorf
neighbours.summary: A small Holstein town where the roads to Schleswig, Lübeck and Hamburg meet. Unremarkable but for the small ash in its churchyard, cut down every New Year's Night by a white rider while a black rider fails to stop him.

neighbours.name: Lübeck
neighbours.summary: Germany's most important coastal port and one of its richest cities, the hub of Baltic trade, set on an oval island at the mouth of the Trave ringed by moat canals. Henry the Lion founded it in effect in 1157, built the harbour, made it a bishopric and granted the Statutes of Lübeck: self-rule by a merchants' council under an Älderman with its own justice, whose taxes pay for proud civic works, including a great brick cathedral at the south tip due within a decade. Furs, leather, timber, amber and iron ore come in; salt, spices, grain, herring, cloth and metalware go out, and a large fleet fishes off Scania under a profitable herring monopoly. Its merchants have kept a trading counter in Novgorod since 1205. The city has an ordinary Divine aura and is the home of Oculus Septentrionalis, of the Goldenes Kalb tavern and of the Novgorod Inn at the north end of town. Under Danish rule until 1227, when it is expected to become a Free Imperial City and, in time, the leading city of the Hanseatic League.

neighbours.name: Rostock
neighbours.summary:
A growing Baltic port in Mecklenburg, overshadowed by Lübeck, and the chief town of the Sorbian princes of Mecklenburg. Valdemar I burnt it in 1161 and drove its Radegast-worshippers into the countryside, and it is now mostly German.

Secrets
The Mecklenburg family still worship Radegast in secret; see their record and the Cult of Radegast.

neighbours.name: Münster
neighbours.summary: A prosperous market city at the centre of the flat, highly fertile Münsterland in Westphalia. It grew from the monastery founded in 805 as a base for converting the Saxons, and its cathedral is St Liudger's.

neighbours.name: Dortmund
neighbours.summary: A Westphalian town known among those who know of such things as the principal seat of the Holy Vehm, the secret courts of the north.

neighbours.name: Paderborn
neighbours.summary: A Saxon town built round hundreds of tiny warm springs that form the source of the little River Pader. Here in 799 Charlemagne met Pope Leo III and the founding of the Holy Roman Empire was agreed; Charlemagne began a lofty cathedral and a palace for it, and the palace is now a ruin after fires in 1000 and 1165. The Externsteine stand on the edge of the Teutoburger Forest nearby, and the abbey of Corvey lies twenty miles east.

neighbours.name: Bremen
neighbours.summary: A port on the north bank of the Weser and the oldest Saxon bishopric, its first church built in 789 after Charlemagne sent Willehad to the Saxons; the see came here from Hamburg. The market traders have long held independent rights, and Archbishop Gerhard II contends with them for control of the city. The cursed, misted peat waste of the Teufelsmoor lies to the north-east.

neighbours.name: Lüneburg
neighbours.summary: A Saxon town built over extensive salt mines that have made it very rich, with grand brick buildings, though subsidence tilts the houses over rickety streets, and a planned great brick cathedral is of doubtful wisdom. Its salt goes out through Hamburg. The open Lüneburg Heath, where shepherds keep the goat-like Heidschnucken, lies to the south.

neighbours.name: Hildesheim
neighbours.summary: Called the jewel of northern Germany. In 815 Louis the Pious hung relics of the Virgin on a rosebush while hunting; they could not be removed, so he founded a church, and the rosebush still grows in a cloister by the cathedral. St Bernward, bishop early in the eleventh century and adviser to Otto II, established the Romanesque style here and left magnificent churches and civic buildings, artists and architects. The greatest church is St Michael on its own hill north of the cathedral, with six towers, many relics and paintings, and Bernward's crypt.

neighbours.name: Brunswick
neighbours.summary: Henry the Lion's residence in the twelfth century, adorned with art and monuments: the bronze Burglöwe lion stands in the central square, the fortress-like cathedral begun in 1173 is now complete and rich, in a style other Welf churches have copied, and beside it is Henry's fortress Burg Dankwarderode, named for the city's heroic founder.

neighbours.name: Goslar
neighbours.summary: A Free Imperial City on the northern edge of the Harz, famed for the Rammelsberg silver mines, Germany's largest and a prized imperial asset, now slowly flooding because spiteful gnomes have turned an underground river into them. Henry the Lion's claim to these mines led Barbarossa to strip him of his estates. Whoever drains the mines would be richly rewarded by the emperor.

neighbours.name: Quedlinburg
neighbours.summary: Henry the Fowler's effective capital for a generation early in the tenth century, with a castle on the Burgberg at the south end and a palace that has hosted Imperial Diets. The abbesses of the foundation for noblewomen that his widow Mathilde established have ruled the town since. It is now overshadowed by the greater Saxon cities.

neighbours.name: Magdeburg
neighbours.summary: Otto the Great's favoured city on the west bank of the Elbe, an archbishopric since 962 and the centre of Church authority over the Eastern Marches. The Magdeburg Law, with its generous charters and quick local courts, encourages new settlements in the east. The forgotten stone circle of the Teufelsküche lies deep in the Haldensleben Forest to the north-west.

neighbours.name: Louis IV, Landgrave of Thuringia
neighbours.summary: Louis IV, called the Pious, is landgrave of Thuringia, seated at the Wartburg near Eisenach, the ancestral castle founded in 1067 by Count Louis I and never breached. His father Hermann I, who ruled from 1190 to 1217, made it a famous court of literature and music on the French model, with lavish festivals and travelling minnesänger. Louis is to marry Elisabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary, who was raised amid the Wartburg's splendour and finds it empty, giving herself in secret to the poor and sick; stopped once with bread for beggars in her apron, she opened it to show roses. If history holds, Louis dies in 1227, Elisabeth founds a hospice at Marburg, dies in 1231 and is canonised in 1235, and the Teutonic Knights raise a great church over her hospice.

neighbours.name: Imperial Abbey of Hersfeld
neighbours.summary: One of the largest and most important abbeys in Germany, founded in the eighth century by Lullus, archbishop of Mainz. The springs it was built round are known for restorative powers of a magical kind; they and the giant bell in the Katharinenturm are both named for Lullus. Its rival Fulda lies forty miles south.

neighbours.name: Abbey of Fulda
neighbours.summary: The huge and wealthy monastery that holds the grave of St Boniface, the martyred English monk, and so a major place of pilgrimage. The Michaelskirche at the town's centre copies the Holy Sepulchre as a Greek cross, and four monastic churches outside the town at the compass points form a giant cross; the eastern one, the Peterskirche on its hill, holds the crypt of St Lioba, Boniface's kinswoman. It rivals Hersfeld.

neighbours.name: Bishop of Würzburg
neighbours.summary: A bishopric since the eighth century. The cathedral holds the shrine of St Kilian, the seventh-century Irish missionary and martyr who first brought the faith here and is popularly the patron of wine, for the bishop is master of Franconia's largest vineyards. He has begun a huge rectangular fortress on the Marienberg across the Main as his future residence.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Bamberg
neighbours.summary: Emperor Henry II made Bamberg a bishopric in 1007 and founded the cathedral on the chief of its seven hills, where he is buried.

neighbours.name: Abbey of the Petersberg, Erfurt
neighbours.summary: The Benedictine abbey on Erfurt's Petersberg, where Barbarossa often held court. Erfurt's other hill, the Domhügel, carries the eighth-century Marienkirche.

neighbours.name: Eisenach
neighbours.summary: The town beneath the Wartburg, the landgraves' never-breached castle. Under Hermann I the castle became a centre of poetry and song; at the Sängerkrieg of 1204 Walther von der Vogelweide beat every rival, Wolfram von Eschenbach and Henry von Ofterdingen among them. Walther then wrote for Philip of Swabia and for Otto of Brunswick, helping the latter to the throne by 1209. The fashionable epics are the Nibelungenlied, made for the court of Passau, Tristan und Isold, Parzival and the Gudrunlied, beside courtly verse of chaste devotion to an unattainable lady.

neighbours.name: Erfurt
neighbours.summary: Thuringia's oldest and largest town, held by the archbishops of Mainz, from which St Boniface set out to the Slavs. It rises on two hills: the Domhügel with the eighth-century Marienkirche and the Petersberg with its Benedictine abbey. Frederick II's court has visited four times between 1214 and 1220. Its wealth comes from exporting woad for blue dye.

neighbours.name: Naumburg
neighbours.summary: A well-fortified, scenic town high above the Saale in eastern Thuringia, originally the New Castle the Ekkehardinger counts built when they moved their seat across the river in the tenth century. It has its own bishop and a prosperous market, and has just begun a large cathedral of St Peter and St Paul. The young and secretive sculptor-architect known as the Master of Naumburg, German-born, French-trained and rumoured to owe his unmatched work to sorcery or divine inspiration, is expected to leave great works here, at Mainz and at Meissen.

neighbours.name: Hersfeld
neighbours.summary: A town on the border of Thuringia and Hesse wholly dominated by its huge imperial abbey, whose springs are held to heal and whose giant bell hangs in the Katharinenturm.

neighbours.name: Fritzlar
neighbours.summary: A Hessian town. A little to the north, near Züschen, stands the Riesenstein, the stone the Devil threw at the church-building villagers of Neueburg and wept bloody tears on; the hidden glade of the Donar Oak at Geismar lies somewhere in the wilderness nearby.

neighbours.name: Frankfurt
neighbours.summary:
A city of some ten thousand on the Main whose bridge is the gateway between north and south Germany. Charlemagne founded it in the eighth century after a fog-hidden ford, shown by deer, saved his retreating army from the Saxons, and built a fortress on the Römerberg over an older Roman site. After the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it was the capital of Louis the German, who founded St Saviour's in 852; it declined in the eleventh century, and the Hohenstaufen revived and fortified it, so that it now hosts imperial elections. The Römerberg square holds markets, fairs, tournaments and coronation festivals, and Italian banking houses keep offices here. In 1220 Frederick II holds here his last German Diet for fifteen years.

On the road from Durenmar to the Gorge, between the Odenwald and Mainz, with a large market fair.

neighbours.name: Fulda
neighbours.summary: The pilgrimage town of St Boniface's grave, in a long valley between the bright wooded Vogelsberg to the west and the impenetrable Rhön to the east, laid out as a giant cross of churches round its wealthy abbey.

neighbours.name: Wimpfen
neighbours.summary: A favoured imperial residence high above the Neckar, held in turn by the Romans, the Franks and the bishops of Worms until Barbarossa took it in the twelfth century. The imperial palace stands where the Roman frontier fort had its temple of Mercury; the walls carry towers each of a different colour, the Roter Turm of red sandstone and the Blauer Turm of blue limestone among them. The bishop of Worms's administrator still lives in the grand Wormser Hof with much land and influence. The lower town clusters round the Stiftskirche and a Benedictine abbey by an ancient Neckar bridge, and the fertile wine hills of the Stromberg lie south.

neighbours.name: Neustadt an der grossen Linden
neighbours.summary: A free trading post in Franconia that has stayed a quiet backwater under its guardian lime tree, whose spirit has taken the townsfolk for its realm. The tree's siege-ruined branches rest on stone columns and monuments carved with the arms of the princes who fought there, and the townsfolk will not clear their woods. Prophecy says the town loses its freedom when the tree dies.

neighbours.name: Würzburg
neighbours.summary: An influential episcopal city of artists and scholars on the Main in central Franconia, amid the region's largest vineyards; wine is its export and St Kilian, whose shrine is in the cathedral, its patron. The bishop's new fortress rises on the Marienberg across the river. Peter von Würzburg of Fengheld takes his name from here.

neighbours.name: Bamberg
neighbours.summary: Henry II's city on seven hills, built from 1007 to rival Rome and far smaller, but keeping a spacious grandeur. Beer is its export: more than a dozen breweries, the oldest and largest of them the Bierhaus, older than the city and of legendary quality. East of it lie the weathered granite blocks of the Luisenburg and the empty Fichtelgebirge.

neighbours.name: Nuremberg
neighbours.summary: Among Franconia's youngest cities yet arguably its most important, home to the Kaiserburg on its sandstone hill, an unofficial capital and the Empire's treasury, where by custom each new emperor holds his first Diet. Barbarossa and lately Frederick II have added wings and towers, and the upper level of the Kaiserkapelle is for the emperor alone. A crossroads trading city exporting linen, with many carpenters who make looms. The Harberg, with its wandering Drudenbaum, overlooks it.

neighbours.name: Regensburg
neighbours.summary: The principal city of the Danube in Bavaria. The Rhine Tribunal's Bavarian lands stop at the river; Regensburg, the other Danube cities and everything south of it are claimed by the Greater Alps Tribunal.

neighbours.name: Mestwin I of Pomerania
neighbours.summary: Prince of Pomerania, a thinly peopled Slavic land between the Baltic and Poland that has been part of the Empire only since 1181, when Barbarossa made Bogislaw a duke. Mestwin rules under an oath of allegiance to Valdemar II of Denmark. He is old, with four sons; the eldest, Swantopolk, is expected to succeed him as duke. German settlers are arriving, the Church is weak here, and the Knights of the Sword found towns and monasteries and hunt pagan remnants in the forests.

neighbours.name: Albert II, Margrave of Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: Margrave of the low, forested march east of the Elbe that Albert the Bear, a Saxon, founded in 1150 after his campaigns against the Wends, and that his Ascanian descendants have ruled since. Its people are a thorough mix of Germans and Wends, and the forest is slowly being cleared for farms. Albert II is old; his heir is Otto, called the Pious.

neighbours.name: Dietrich the Oppressed, Margrave of Meissen
neighbours.summary: Wettin margrave of Meissen, a dynasty ruling since 1089, who also rules the march of Lusatia. Meissen is the most civilised part of the Marches, rolling, moderately peopled, fully German and a political and ecclesiastical backwater; Lusatia is forest wilderness peopled only by Sorbs. No Hermetic covenant has stood in Meissen since Sirmium fell to the Magyars in the tenth century, and the vis sources the Order knew there perished with it.

neighbours.name: Bishop Absalon of Roskilde
neighbours.summary: The Danish bishop of Roskilde who rode with Valdemar I's invasion of Rügen in 1168 and in 1169 destroyed the fortress-temple of Arkona, the holiest site of the sun-god Svantovit. The Danish Church brought the faith to the island, where it is still new.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: The first bishopric east of the Elbe, founded in 948 by Otto the Great and briefly lost to a Slavic counter-attack later that century. Albert the Bear rebuilt the cathedral on the middle of Brandenburg's three islands.

neighbours.name: Marienkirche of Bergen
neighbours.summary: The church of Bergen, the only town on Rügen. With the Pfarrkirche at Altenkirchen it is one of the two churches of note on the island.

neighbours.name: Pfarrkirche of Altenkirchen
neighbours.summary: One of Rügen's two churches of note, on the windswept northern peninsula of Wittow, where two last priests of Svantovit scrape a living.

neighbours.name: Cistercian monastery of Rügen
neighbours.summary: A monastery founded after the Danish conquest of 1168. Its monks have only just begun farming the Mönchgut peninsula, which takes its new name from them, and a church is planned at Sagard, five miles from Crintera, which would push the Dominion toward the covenant.

neighbours.name: Bergen
neighbours.summary: The only town of any size on Rügen, founded by the Danes and ruled by them, with the Marienkirche. The islanders are mostly Slavic, Christianity is new, and the Danes have requisitioned every horse on the island.

neighbours.name: Stettin
neighbours.summary: A small port on the Oder below an old Wendish fortress, the ancestral seat of the Pomeranian rulers. Germans have settled since the middle of the twelfth century and paid for the church of St Jakob, finished in 1187.

neighbours.name: Brandenburg
neighbours.summary: The only notable city of the margravate east of the Elbe, on the site of an old Wendish settlement across three adjacent islands in the Havel; the middle island carries the cathedral Albert the Bear rebuilt.

neighbours.name: Meissen
neighbours.summary: Seat of the margravate, on the left bank of the Elbe below the Burgberg, the stronghold Henry I founded in 929. A bishopric since 963, with a prosperous market where German merchants meet traders from Lusatia, Silesia and Poland, but not yet rich enough for a cathedral. Upstream the limestone pinnacles of the Bastei rise a thousand feet over the river.

neighbours.name: Freiberg
neighbours.summary: The largest of the new mining towns of the Ore Mountains, founded in 1186 after silver and tin were found in that bleak evergreen range; a twelfth-century imperial decree lets anyone prospect there and keep the proceeds. Its merchants travel to Prague by the bridges at Most.

neighbours.name: Bautzen
neighbours.summary: The one place in Lusatia with real German influence, not far from Meissen. The Peace of Bautzen in 1018 ceded the area from Henry II to Boleslaus I of Poland, and it returned to the Empire in 1033. The Knights of the Sword keep a large fortification here where slaves, mostly Pomeranian, are held before being taken south to the market at Prague.

neighbours.name: King Otakar of Bohemia
neighbours.summary: Premyslid king of Bohemia, a semi-autonomous subject kingdom of the Empire that Barbarossa raised from a duchy a generation ago. His house has ruled since the eighth century, descended from the farmer Premysl whom the Gifted princess Libuse chose by vision at Vysehrad. The margrave of Moravia, the Empire's easternmost march on the Hungarian border, is usually the king's son or brother. Bohemia has no great cities, only modest towns round and north of Prague, living by farming, hunting, mining, glass, brewing and horses; many more towns are expected to be founded through the century as German feudal ways replace the Slavic chiefdoms.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St Vitus, Prague
neighbours.summary: The seat of the bishopric of Prague, created in 973 under Mainz with Thietmar of Merseburg as its first bishop. Inside the castle, it holds the shrine and grave of St Wenceslaus and relics of St Adalbert. The Basilica of St George, with its convent, stands beside it.

neighbours.name: Strahov monastery
neighbours.summary: An austere Premonstratensian house near Prague Castle, founded in 1140.

neighbours.name: Sedlec monastery
neighbours.summary: A Cistercian monastery a couple of dozen miles south-east of Prague, founded in 1142. A monk named Anton, napping after work in the vineyard, woke to find three rods of silver sprouting beside his head and left his frock, his kutna, to mark the spot; the monks have just opened a mine there of fantastically rich deposits. If history holds, a wealthy royal town grows up round it later in the century and takes Goslar's place as the Empire's chief source of silver. A far-sighted magus might buy the land for a trifle and mine it by magic, until Bohemian merchants notice prices rising and the Quaesitores take an interest.

neighbours.name: Prague
neighbours.summary: Bohemia's chief settlement and the ancestral seat of its rulers, founded late in the ninth century on the Vltava at the land's centre; small by German standards at about three thousand people. Prague Castle on its hill over the west bank encloses the basilicas of St George and St Vitus, with Strahov monastery nearby, and a second castle stands on Vysehrad rock just south. Since the eleventh century the city has spread to the east bank, with a market run mostly by German merchants and a small Jewish quarter. It exports cheap glassware to northern Germany and holds a large slave market.

neighbours.name: Most
neighbours.summary: A town and market south of the Ore Mountains, grown up round the maze of wooden bridges over swampy ground that lets merchants pass between Freiberg and Prague; its name means Bridge.

neighbours.name: Brünn
neighbours.summary: Seat of the Premyslid margraves of Moravia, where a castle and the church of St Michael were founded on Petrov Hill early in the eleventh century at the meeting of the Svitava and Svratka; a market town and mines have grown round them, and a handful of German settlers have lately arrived. In the town hall hangs the stuffed carcass of the Dragon of Brünn, which generations ago ate townsfolk from a cave by the Svratka until a travelling butcher fed it an ox hide sewn full of unslaked lime; it drank from the river and burst. Whether he was a butcher, a wizard or a magus in disguise nobody knows.

neighbours.name: The Hansas
neighbours.summary: Associations of merchants for mutual protection, the settling of disputes and agreed prices, which have existed since at least the twelfth century but remain small. If history holds, a treaty between Lübeck and Hamburg in 1241, sharing the cost of guarding the Trave and Elbe against robbers and punishing crimes against each other's burgesses, becomes the first great one; scores of German and Baltic cities join over the following decades, and by 1300 the League is rich and powerful under Lübeck's lead, fighting pirates with bigger ships, convoys, hired armies and noble allies. Whether Oculus Septentrionalis stands at its heart, and whether Imanitos Mendax plants corruption there, is for the storyguide.

details.wants: Protection from robbers and pirates; agreed prices; justice for their burgesses abroad
details.offers: Mutual protection, settlement of disputes and price agreements among member merchants

neighbours.name: The Holy Vehm
neighbours.summary:
A system of secret courts, mainly in northern Germany and seated at Dortmund, claiming the power of life and death from an imperial mandate of Charlemagne. Its members, the Wissende, number tens of thousands: any free, legitimately born man who is neither excommunicate nor outlaw may be initiated. It works by secret meetings, kidnappings by night, hostile trials and in some regions torture, and passes one sentence, hanging in a public place with an SSGG knife left by the corpse. Its officers are the Stuhlherr, usually the local secular or church lord; the Freigraf, appointed for life, who truly rules the court; the Freischöffen who accuse and decide; the Fronboten who execute; and the Fehmenotes, secret informants across the Empire. Its supreme head is the archbishop of Cologne. Philippus Niger of Durenmar has assured House Guernicus that it poses no danger to the Order.

Secrets
Philippus Niger uses the Vehm: two of his trusted men are Freigrafs and he knows more than twenty Fehmenotes. He has had dozens of suspected hedge wizards and at least one Marched magus hanged by its courts, and is spreading it southward as a weapon against hedge wizards. He has no grounds for his assurance to House Guernicus.
neighbours.ruler: The archbishop of Cologne, as Oberststuhlherr

details.rules: Members swear to uphold the Vehm, keep its secrets even from kin and report everything; each receives a rope and a knife marked SSGG. Courts sit on a hillock or known spot, lately also in vast underground chambers, and intruders are killed. An accused who does not appear is condemned if the accuser brings seven character witnesses, without the charge being examined; one who appears needs twenty-one to be acquitted; a member clears himself by oath unless charged with betraying the Vehm. Women, children, Jews, heathens and in practice nobles are exempt.
details.wants: The Blutbann, the power of life and death, which it says the nobility has usurped
details.offers: Judgement on heresy, witchcraft, perjury, murder and sacrilege where the lords will not act

neighbours.name: The Witches of the Harz
neighbours.summary: Cunning-folk who venerate Walpurga as a goddess and keep the old ways with dozens of traditional villagers. They hold council on the Hexentanzplatz crag every April and go on to the Brocken on Walpurgis Night, 30 April, to light fires and sing to forgotten gods while Walpurga calls up the spirits of summer against winter's; only the most powerful may approach the Witches' Altar at the summit. Their design is left to the storyguide, as folk with minor powers of potion and charm; they can never cast true spells or work major magic, or the Order would long since have absorbed or destroyed them. Magi know the gatherings as a good place to find a potential apprentice.

details.rules: Council at the Hexentanzplatz each April; only the strongest approach the Witches' Altar
details.wants: To venerate Walpurga and keep the old ways of the villages
details.offers: Potions, charms and the goddess's favour; a place where magi find apprentices

neighbours.name: Priesthood of Woden
neighbours.summary: Tall red-bearded priests in long white cloaks who once came to the forgotten stone circle of the Teufelsküche, deep in the Haldensleben Forest north-west of Magdeburg, in the hour before dawn with men in skins and darker shapes, to slaughter a sacrifice and burn its vitals to herald the day. The missionaries who purged the cult named the place the Devil's Kitchen. Whether any of the priests survive is for the storyguide; the Wild Hunt rises from the same stones.

neighbours.name: Cult of Radegast
neighbours.summary:
The worship of Radegast, the Slavic god of chieftainship and war, and also of fertility and harvest. His worship was anciently centred in Pomerania at his Oracle in the fortress-temple of Rethra, now ruined and plundered, though Mount Radhost in Moravia was always his sacred site and the Ex Miscellanea half of Roznov is his priesthood, with Igor Rastvan as high priest. His devotees are often tied to noble or royal pagan families and serve as court advisers; his favoured are inspiring and commanding, and overconfident. The princes of Mecklenburg were driven from his open worship in 1161.

Secrets
The Mecklenburg nobility still come secretly to Rethra to honour Radegast and have gained powers from him; Imanitos Mendax poses as the god's prophet to them. In the saga plot Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea, Radegast is a demon. At Roznov the summer-solstice festival hides human sacrifices.
neighbours.ruler: Igor Rastvan of Roznov, high priest

details.wants: A kingdom of the Slavs united under Radegast
details.offers: Temporal influence at pagan courts; the god's favour to the inspired and the overconfident

neighbours.name: Pirates of Frisia
